result.summary: The poet invokes Apollo and explains how Pelias, warned by an oracle, sent Jason on the quest for the golden fleece. The heroes are catalogued as they gather, then they leave Iolcus amid the grief of Alcimede, choose Jason as leader, launch the Argo and sacrifice to Apollo, where Idmon prophesies and Idas boasts.

scenes.title: Invocation and Pelias's oracle
scenes.summary: The poet begins with Apollo and tells how Pelias, warned of a one-sandalled man, devised the voyage for Jason.
scenes.stakes: Pelias fears being killed by the man with one sandal; Jason is sent into peril.

scenes.title: Catalogue of the heroes
scenes.summary: The heroes who join Jason are named one by one with their lineages and homelands.
scenes.stakes: Several heroes are fated to die far from home, such as Canthus and Mopsus.

scenes.title: Heroes march to the ship
scenes.summary: The heroes walk through the city to Pagasae while the townspeople lament.
scenes.stakes: The heroes face a hard voyage; the people fear they will not return.

scenes.title: Alcimede's farewell
scenes.summary: Alcimede weeps and clings to Jason, who comforts her before leaving.
scenes.stakes: Alcimede stands to lose her only son.

scenes.title: Assembly and choice of leader
scenes.summary: On the beach Heracles refuses leadership and Jason is chosen to lead.
scenes.stakes: The quest could be hindered by division.

scenes.title: Launching the Argo and sacrifice
scenes.summary: The heroes launch the ship, assign benches, and sacrifice to Apollo. Idmon prophesies return for most but death for himself.
scenes.stakes: Idmon foresees his own death in Asia.

scenes.title: Feast and Idas's boast
scenes.summary: At the beach feast, Jason is gloomy and Idas boasts that nothing will defeat them.
scenes.stakes: Jason's morale and the unity of the crew.

alias_notes.explanation: Apollo is identified by his mother Leto.
Phoebus is a title of Apollo, 'bright one'.

notable_quotes.reason: Opening line of the epic, invoking Apollo and announcing the quest.
Idas's arrogant boast that his spear matters more than Zeus's help.

analysis.text: The opening sets up the quest as a commission born of fear and fate, and the long catalogue shows heroism as a gathering of kin, skills and destinies.
The catalogue of heroes follows Homer's Catalogue of Ships, and flatters many Greek regions by tying their lineages to the voyage.

legacy.text: Apollonius's epic influenced Roman poets such as Virgil, whose Aeneid draws on the Argonautica, and Valerius Flaccus, who wrote a Latin Argonautica.
The film Jason and the Argonauts (1963) retells the quest, with effects by Ray Harryhausen.

fun_facts.text: The poem was written by Apollonius of Rhodes in the 3rd century BC, probably while he worked at the Library of Alexandria.

language_notes.text: Phoebus is a title of Apollo, meaning 'bright'. 'Behest' means command; 'well-benched' describes a ship with good rowing benches.
The Cyanean rocks are the Clashing Rocks (Symplegades) at the entrance to the Black Sea, which crushed passing ships. Pontus is the Black Sea.
'With but one sandal' refers to a man wearing a single sandal; the oracle warned Pelias to beware of him.
Pelias neglected Hera, which explains her later hostility to him and her support of Jason.
'Lose his home-return' means fail to return home; Pelias hoped the voyage would kill Jason.
'Aeson's son' is a patronymic for Jason. Cheiron is the wise centaur who raised Jason.
Caeneus was invulnerable; the Centaurs piled pine trees on him and buried him alive.
The Far-shooting god is Apollo. Eurytus, a master archer, challenged Apollo to a contest and was killed.
Theseus and Peirithous went down to the underworld to seize Persephone and were held there.
"Nor do we learn that..." is a litotes-like narrator's formula: Heracles did indeed answer Jason's call promptly.
Refers to Heracles' labour of bringing the Erymanthian boar alive to Eurystheus, king of Mycenae, who set his labours.
"If the report is true" is the poet's hedge, distancing himself from the marvel of seeing beneath the earth.
Periclymenus's gift from Poseidon is shape-shifting, so he could take any form he wished in battle.
"Imbrasion" means of the river Imbrasos, an epithet of Hera at her Samian sanctuary.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose".
Boreas, the North Wind, carried off the Athenian princess Oreithyia; "Cecropia" is an old name for Attica.
"Minyae" is the name of an ancient people of Orchomenus and Iolcus, here used for the whole crew.
Thralls are servants or slaves who here prepare the ship's supplies.
The townspeople say "King Zeus" as an exclamation. The translation keeps the Greek name Zeus here, as it does elsewhere in this passage.
"Panachaean land" means all of Achaea, i.e. Greece. "Whither" means "to where."
The golden fleece is in Colchis, ruled by Aeetes. The speakers fear the heroes will burn his palace if he will not hand it over.
Refers to Phrixus and Helle fleeing on the golden ram. Helle fell into the sea, and the ram spoke. The fleece sought now comes from this ram.
Thralls are slaves or bonded household servants.
"Baleful" here means miserable and sorrowful, describing the old father Aeson's painful old age.
"Loosed my virgin zone" means she lost her virginity; the zone was the girdle a maiden wore until marriage.
Eileithyia was the goddess of childbirth; Alcimede says she denied her more children.
Phrixus fled on the golden ram to Colchis. His flight led to the quest for the Fleece, which sends Jason away.
"A bird of ill omen" means someone whose weeping might bring bad luck to the voyage.
Delos, Claros, Pytho and Lyeia by the Xanthus were famous seats of Apollo's worship and oracles.
"Hasting" means hastening; the crew are surprised that Aeastus and Argus come quickly, though Pelias would not approve of their joining.
"Mantle of double fold" is a cloak folded double for warmth, a fine garment as opposed to Argus's rough bull's hide.
"Common to all is our return" means everyone shares the same risks and outcome; therefore the leader should be chosen by all with a generous heart.
"Propitiate" means to win the favour of a god, here through sacrifice before the voyage.
"Thralls" are servants or slaves; "steading" is a farmstead or estate.
Embasius means "of embarking"; Apollo is invoked as protector of those boarding ships. The oracle refers to his earlier prophecy to Jason at Delphi.
The rope girded round the hull from bow to stern, tightened to hold the planks together; this was a known ancient practice for strengthening ships.
A cubit is an ancient measure of about the length of a forearm, roughly 18 inches. Thole-pins are pegs that hold oars in place.
Shingle means coarse beach pebbles. Actius means 'of the shore' and Embasius 'of embarkation', titles of Apollo as protector of sailors.
Pytho is Delphi, site of Apollo's oracle, where Jason consulted the god before the voyage. Hellas means Greece.
Far-darter is an epithet of Apollo, the archer god.
Leto's son is Apollo; Idmon is his prophet-son, so he reads the god's will in the sacrificial flame and smoke.
Idas's claim that his spear helps him more than Zeus does is a boast of impiety, hinting at his arrogance.

context_notes.text: Orpheus was the legendary Thracian singer, son of the Muse Calliope, whose music moved even nature.
Peleus and Telamon exiled themselves after killing their half-brother Phocus (spelled Phoeus here); Peleus later fathered Achilles.
Tiphys becomes the helmsman of the Argo, valued for his skill at reading weather and stars.
"She" is Athena, who in tradition helped design the Argo; Argus was its builder.
Idmon is a seer whose true father is Apollo (Leto's son), who gave him prophecy.
Polydeuces and Castor are the Dioscuri; Leda bore them, though Polydeuces was usually said to be fathered by Zeus.
Hephaestus was the divine smith and himself lame, which explains his son's crippled feet.
Pytho is Delphi, home of Apollo's oracle, which Jason consulted before sailing.
Pagasae was a port in Magnesia, in Thessaly, from which the Argo is said to have sailed.
Alcimede is the mother of Jason. Aeson is his aged father, who was set aside by Pelias.
Pelias, king of Iolcus, ordered Jason to fetch the Golden Fleece, hoping he would die trying.
Iphias was a priestess of Artemis, protector of Iolcus, who here honors the departing hero.
Pagasae was a port in Thessaly where the Argo was built and launched; the Argonauts gather there.
Heracles was the most famous and strongest hero among the crew, so the Argonauts naturally look to him first.
Phoebus is a name for Apollo, god of prophecy, whose favour the voyage depends on.
Heracles, the strongest hero, and Ancaeus sit at the middle bench, where the strongest rowers sat.
Greeks burned the thigh bones wrapped in fat for the gods and ate the remaining meat themselves.
Arene was a town in Messenia, the home of Idas.

literary_notes.text: The epic opens by calling on Apollo, following the tradition of beginning with a god's blessing and stating the subject.
The oak trees at Zone are offered as living proof of Orpheus's power, explaining a place's features through myth.
The poet reveals in advance that Canthus and Mopsus will die in Libya, shadowing the voyage with loss.
The distance between sunrise and sunset stresses how far from home the heroes' graves lie, with a gnomic remark on fate.
Praising the Argo as the best of all oared ships magnifies the voyage and its heroes.
Idmon knows he will die yet goes anyway, for the sake of renown, a tragic heroic choice.
Euphemus running across the sea without wetting his feet is a marvelous exaggeration of his speed.
Vivid visual detail of gleaming wings and wind-blown hair makes the sons of Boreas striking and semi-divine.
This summary closes the catalogue, with the poet marking its completion before turning to the next stage.
The heroes are compared to gleaming stars among clouds, stressing their brilliance against the dull crowd.
The narrator reports the crowd's speech and prayers, so public worry frames the voyage before it begins.
Death is called better than living on, since it would spare Aeson the grief his son's voyage will bring.
Alcimede's clinging grief is compared to a mistreated orphan girl weeping on her old nurse's neck, giving the pain a vivid human picture.
The flight of Phrixus seemed remote and harmless to her, yet it brings the loss of her son.
Jason is likened to Apollo leaving his shrine, stressing his godlike beauty and heroic radiance.
The priestess left behind is compared to the old left by the young, ending the scene on a note of pathos.
The contrast between the rough bull's hide and the fine mantle quickly sketches the two newcomers' differing appearance and status.
Heracles' blunt prohibition shows his commanding strength and his willingness to put the expedition's purpose above personal glory.
"Warlike Jason" and "bold Heracles" use stock descriptive epithets typical of epic style.
Idmon's announcement of his death in Asia prepares for his later death on the voyage.
Jason is compared to a man weighed down by thought, showing his helpless anxiety as leader.
Idas's boasting and defiance of the gods reveal his brash, arrogant nature, in contrast with Jason's doubt.
